perspective:
I, Vincent Chinana, have access to the following:

- I am an Alaska Native mechanic. Patrick Guzman is my long-time friend; we met as teenagers and often combine my mechanical skills with his construction expertise.
- At a local diner, Patrick told me he was considering a new construction venture to expand his business. He said it seemed like a good opportunity, that he thought it was worth the risk, and that he was still weighing his options. I told him I had heard it was risky, was worried about financial security, and advised him to reconsider or delay until he gathered more information. He appreciated my concern and said he would think it over more.
- Over the next few days, I noticed Patrick avoiding detailed discussions about the investment. At his construction site, I told him I felt he was not telling me everything and that I felt betrayed. He said it was complicated, that he did not want to worry me, apologized, said he should have been more open, and offered to sit down and explain everything.
- During a detailed discussion at my garage, I learned the situation was serious. Patrick told me it had been tough and that he might lose a significant amount if it did not turn around soon. I offered to lend him money to cover short-term losses. He thanked me and said he was grateful for my support.
- A month later, at a coffee shop, I understood the venture might actually turn a profit. I said so, apologized for doubting Patrick earlier, and proposed a joint venture because I saw potential. Patrick agreed and said we should work out the details.
- Now Patrick and I are optimistic about the joint venture. At my house, we met to draft a business plan. I said that combining our skills could make it a success; Patrick said he was excited. I said we should outline every step carefully, and Patrick agreed we should cover all our bases and set it up for success.
